definition: The water-soluble, serine-rich glycoprotein gum that coats and binds the two fibroin strands of a raw silk filament and is largely removed during degumming.
explanation: A raw silk filament is two fibroin brins wrapped in layers of sericin. The gum glues the filament into the cocoon structure and makes raw silk stiffer and less lustrous than finished silk. Sericin is hydrophilic because many of its amino acids carry polar side groups, especially serine, aspartic acid and glycine residues, and it dissolves in hot water, particularly with soap, alkali or enzymes. Degumming exploits this solubility, removing most of the sericin to reveal the softer, brighter fibroin beneath. Because sericin is a large fraction of cocoon mass, its removal has a major effect on yarn weight.
example: A weaver weighs a skein of raw silk, degums it in a hot soap bath, dries it and weighs it again, recording a loss of roughly a quarter of the original mass. Most of that loss is sericin. Another skein is only partly degummed, leaving some gum in place, and it keeps a crisper, firmer hand. The exercise shows that degumming is a controllable finishing choice rather than an all-or-nothing step.
caution: Sericin content varies with silkworm strain and with how it is measured, so percentages differ between studies. The extraction method also changes the recovered protein: hot water, soap, alkali and enzymes hydrolyze sericin to different degrees, which is why sericin sold for cosmetic or biomedical use is not one uniform material. Residual sericin on a silk yarn is not a defect in itself, and marketing claims about its skin benefits need separate evidence.
deeper: Sericin makes up roughly 20 to 30% of Bombyx mori cocoon mass. It is encoded by several genes, including Ser1, Ser2 and Ser3, whose alternative splicing produces a family of polypeptides ranging from about 20 to 400 kDa; Ser1 is a single-copy gene of about 23 kb with nine exons. Its 18 amino acids are dominated by residues with hydroxyl, carboxyl and amino side groups, and serine commonly accounts for around 30% of the total, which explains both the name and the protein's strong affinity for water. Conventional soap and detergent degumming partially hydrolyzes sericin and lowers its molecular weight, so protein recovered from degumming wastewater is more degraded than sericin extracted under milder conditions.
origins: The name comes from the Latin sericum, silk, a word linked in classical sources to the Seres, the name Greek and Roman writers gave to the people of the eastern silk-producing lands. Removing the gum from raw silk is an old practice wherever silk was worked, but interest in sericin as a material in its own right is recent. Research since the late 2000s has studied it for cosmetic and biomedical uses, often proposing recovery from degumming effluent that was historically discarded.

definition: Sericulture is the rearing of silkworms, chiefly the domesticated moth Bombyx mori fed on mulberry leaves, to produce cocoons for silk, from egg production through larval feeding to cocoon harvest.
explanation: The cycle begins with eggs from selected parent moths, hatched to coincide with fresh mulberry leaf growth. Larvae feed on mulberry (Morus species) for several weeks, growing enormously, and each then spins a cocoon from one continuous filament. For reeled silk, cocoons are stifled with heat or steam to kill the pupa before the moth emerges and breaks the filament, then dried, sorted and stored for reeling. A small share of the crop is allowed to emerge to supply eggs. Tussah, eri and muga silks come from other moth species and lie outside mulberry sericulture.
example: A cooperative plans its season. From the number of egg layings it expects, it estimates mulberry area, rearing trays and labor for the final larval stage, when leaf demand peaks. It sells fresh cocoons to a reeling unit that assesses quality, since shell ratio, filament length and reelability determine how much raw silk the cocoons will actually yield.
caution: Sericulture covers cocoon production, not reeling, throwing or weaving, which are separate trades. 'Peace silk' or 'ahimsa silk' labels describe letting moths emerge, which usually means the silk is spun rather than reeled; such claims are rarely independently verified, so ask for documentation. 'Mulberry silk' identifies species and host plant, not grade or quality.
deeper: Genomic and mitochondrial studies indicate B. mori was domesticated from the wild moth Bombyx mandarina roughly 5,000 years ago, probably from northern Chinese populations. Resequencing of 40 genomes found 354 protein-coding genes with selection signals, along with reduced polymorphism and increased homozygosity in domesticated lines. Domesticated adults do not fly and depend on human care. A female lays roughly 300 to 500 eggs. According to the FAO, cocoon filaments total about 600 to 1,500 m, of which about 80 percent is typically reelable, and automatic reeling works well with cocoons offering about 60 percent reelability, 1,000 m filament length and a 20 percent shell ratio.
origins: Archaeological evidence places silk in China in the Neolithic; a cocoon recovered from a Yangshao-culture site in Shanxi province is dated to roughly 4000 to 3000 BCE. Silk production later spread well beyond China through trade and migration, becoming established across East, South and Central Asia and eventually Europe. The word sericulture joins a Latin-derived root for silk (sericum) with 'culture' in the sense of cultivation.
